nameStory: The red-spotted admiral gets its name from the beautiful red-orange spots that dot its dark wings, giving it a distinguished, almost military appearance that reminded early naturalists of naval insignia. The 'admiral' part of the name is shared with several related butterflies that all have that same stately, elegant flight pattern and bold wing markings.
description: The red-spotted admiral is a medium-sized butterfly with striking dark blue-black wings adorned with bright red-orange spots and a subtle blue sheen. This beautiful butterfly is actually part of a fascinating species complex that includes both red-spotted purples (like this one) and white admirals, which have prominent white bands across their wings. They're strong fliers with a distinctive gliding flight pattern, and you'll often see them visiting flowers or puddling at mud patches. Adults have a wingspan of about 3-4 inches across.

idTips.label: Wing coloration
idTips.description: Dark blue-black wings that shimmer with an iridescent blue or purple sheen in sunlight, completely lacking any white bands or stripes

idTips.label: Red-orange spots
idTips.description: Bright red to orange spots scattered along the wing edges, most prominent on the hindwings where they form a distinctive row

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Strong, gliding flight with wings held horizontally, often sailing between flap sequences rather than the erratic flutter of many butterflies

idTips.label: Body appearance
idTips.description: Robust, dark body with a fuzzy texture when viewed up close, proportionally stockier than swallowtails

idTips.label: Wing underside
idTips.description: Undersides show more prominent red-orange markings and blue spots, with a lighter overall appearance than the dark upper wings

habitat: Red-spotted admirals prefer woodland edges, clearings, and gardens where they can find both nectar sources and their host plants. Look for them in deciduous and mixed forests, particularly where cherry, willow, aspen, or birch trees grow, as these serve as food plants for their caterpillars. They're often seen along forest roads, in parks, and suburban areas with mature trees.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, with fresh individuals showing the most vibrant colors and intact wing edges. This is when they're most actively seeking mates and laying eggs.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with multiple generations possible. Adults are commonly seen visiting flowers like butterfly bush, milkweed, and rotting fruit. Look for worn individuals alongside fresh ones.
seasonality.fall: The final generation of adults appears, focusing on nectar sources to build energy reserves. Some individuals may look more faded or have damaged wings from the season's activity.
seasonality.winter: No adults present - the species overwinters as caterpillars in rolled leaf shelters or as chrysalids, depending on the generation timing.

funFact: This butterfly is actually a master of disguise - it evolved to mimic the poisonous pipevine swallowtail so perfectly that predators avoid it, even though it's completely harmless! Meanwhile, its close relatives in northern areas kept their white wing bands and don't bother with mimicry at all.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with the dark form of the pipevine swallowtail, which it deliberately mimics. The key difference is that swallowtails have 'tails' on their hindwings and the red-spotted admiral doesn't - remember 'admiral has no tail to tell the tale.' Also, swallowtails have a more erratic, fluttery flight compared to the admiral's steady gliding.
contextualKnowledge: This species showcases one of nature's most dramatic examples of evolutionary flexibility - in the same species, northern populations (white admirals) kept their honest warning colors while southern populations (red-spotted purples) evolved elaborate mimicry. Where their ranges overlap, you can find hybrid individuals with intermediate wing patterns, creating a living laboratory of evolution in action.
compareHints: The red-spotted admiral differs from its close relative, the viceroy, by being significantly larger and lacking the black line that runs across the viceroy's hindwings. Viceroys are also orange and black (mimicking monarchs) while red-spotted admirals are dark with blue iridescence. Both have similar gliding flight patterns, but the red-spotted admiral's size and coloration make it unmistakable once you know what to look for.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The viceroy's closest New England relative is the red-spotted admiral, which looks completely different with its dark wings marked by white bands and blue-spotted hindwings.
